author: Harriet Williamson
title: The Weather Outside Is Frightful. So Is Labour’s Climate Forecast
content:
If you only had to nail down your wheelie bin to stop it blowing across the street this weekend, you were lucky. 




Three days of back-to-back storms – Austen on Friday, followed immediately by Boelo – 

caused flooding

, power cuts for 

almost 83,000 households

 and 

travel chaos

 across swathes of the UK. Winds of over 80mph were recorded, roads were blocked and flood waters surged in 

apocalyptic scenes

. Two men 

were 

killed by falling trees

. 




After a summer of 

extreme temperatures

, drought and 

a food production crisis

, with more than

 2,800 excess deaths

 due to consecutive heatwaves in May and June alone, you’d think the government might be taking a more muscular approach to the climate emergency.




But just days before the UK was plunged into killer-storm territory, Andy Burnham’s government approved new North Sea drilling in the form of the Jackdaw gas field. 



















The Cortado

 





          Get your shot of political analysis from 

Ash Sarkar

 and 

Steven Methven

, every Monday and Friday morning.        

























First name:













Email:













I agree to the 

Privacy Policy





















































      Sign up error: 

. Try again later.
    


























      Thanks for signing up.
    






















Climate experts are clear: 

no new oil and gas fields 

are compatible with keeping global heating around the 1.5°C mark. Jackdaw and the as-yet-unapproved Rosebank oil field, the two new North Sea projects previously 

halted in the courts 

over their climate impact, are not an exception. 




Perhaps more immediately painful as the weather turns (and I sit cradling a hot water bottle like my firstborn child) is the knowledge that gas from Jackdaw will do sweet FA to bring down energy bills at home, 

according to most analysts

. However, it 

is

 a big win for owner and operator Adura, a joint venture between fossil fuel giant Shell and Norwegian firm Equinox, so I guess we can all be pleased for their shareholders. 




And congratulations might be in order for the climate-wreckers once again, with Whitehall 

‘sources’ briefing 

on Saturday night that Burnham and chancellor John Healey are set to “defy eco-zealot Ed Miliband” and approve Rosebank, despite energy secretary 

Miatta Fahnbulleh insisting

 she’s the only one who can make the final decision. 




Rosebank is far bigger and will be 

significantly more damaging

 than Jackdaw, with predicted lifetime emissions of over 200 million tonnes of CO2 (

equivalent to nearly 70% 

of the UK’s total emissions last year). 




If approved, Rosebank’s oil will be sold on the international market for the benefit of its owners, which include a 20% stake for Ithaca Energy (and Ithaca’s majority shareholder, the 

illegal West Bank settlement-facilitating

 Israeli oil and gas firm Delek). If the UK government goes ahead with Rosebank, it could be in breach of the Geneva Conventions – something that should give major pause to an administration 

banning trade

 with illegal Israeli settlements. 




But there’s more incoherence from Burnham’s lot at play here. On one hand, the government is urging us to stockpile tins and buy windup radios,

 citing severe weather

, and then on the other, ignoring the science in favour of 

“taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea”

, which seems to mean little more than capitulating to fossil fuel giants with delusory benefits for the British public. 




While the government waited until after its 

Holborn and St Pancras byelection win 

against Zack Polanski to announce Jackdaw’s approval, Labour may now be feeling diminishing pressure from the embattled party to its left. The Greens, for which climate should be a slam-dunk issue, are sinking into a polling black hole while Labour rides high with

 32% and an eight-point lead, 

according to Ipsos. Labour peer Harriet Harman certainly felt unembarrassed to tout the 

“green argument for Rosebank”

 on Friday – an equivalent to the turkey’s argument to play a central role in Christmas dinner. 




Jackdaw was the smaller fish, and approving it might’ve been a compromise to soothe the more vociferously climate-denying elements of our political and media class, allowing Rosebank to be rejected as a ‘climate red line’ with less pushback. But what’s the point in speculating? Too much of Westminster analysis is a glorified game of ‘guess what’s in teacher’s head’. Burnham’s first budget is looming on Wednesday, and we can soon judge the government by what it 

does

 to tackle the most existential and interconnected issue of our lifetimes (and our children’s and grandchildren’s lifetimes), rather than what imaginary trade-offs we suspect it might make. 




From food prices and energy bills to migration, 

strain on the NHS

 and 

the planet-poisoning consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza

, climate touches everything. Without a survivable climate, the rest is immaterial. New Goalhanger podcast, anyone?

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Lula Wins Historic Comeback in Brazil Despite Far-Right Election Meddling
content:
Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won an unprecedented fourth term – a stunning comeback victory in the face of attempts by far-right opponents to interfere in the election. 




Lula secured 51.79% of the vote in the run-off on Sunday, 4.4 million more votes than his US-backed rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who secured 48.21%. 




The leftwing incumbent was the runner up in the first round of voting on 4 October, and polling showed both candidates were neck and neck ahead of the run-off on Sunday. 




It is the first time since Brazil’s dictatorship ended in the 1980s that a presidential candidate has won an election without coming first in the initial round of voting. 




“This election was a defeat for denialism,” Lula told a jubilant crowd of supporters in São Paulo on Sunday evening. “I want to thank God and to thank you, Brazilian men and women of this country… it was democracy that made this happen.”




Bolsonaro has refused to concede and is calling for Lula’s victory to be annulled. His father, ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting to stage a military coup after losing to Lula in 2022.

author: Novara Media
title: The New Right Is Obsessed With AI, Israel and the Apocalypse
content:
In Brighton, for a special recording of Downstream IRL, Ash Sarkar sat down with Naomi Klein, and organiser, writer and co-founder of the Debt Collective, Astra Taylor. They gathered to discuss their new book, End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World. 




An apocalyptic alliance of religious fundamentalists, billionaire Silicon Valley tech kings and ethno-nationalists is gathering momentum. They aren’t just exploiting collapse, they’re provoking and accelerating it, whilst protecting themselves from the fallout. The world’s fate is increasingly in the hands of men who are ambivalent about its survival and betting money on the end.




Already, anger at the building of data centres is cutting across left and right, in a way that climate politics rarely has – but how do we make sure that anger is heard? How do we separate necessary alarm from fatalism? And what can we prepare for the impending AI crash?

author: Novara Media
title: The Mao Era – Catastrophe or Necessity?
content:
No one is disputed like Mao. Was he a mass murderer, a Communist hero, a charlatan, or a great poet? The saviour of the peasants, or the man who extracted from them all that he could?




Mao’s biography is a nest of contradictions. He led the largest revolution in world history, then presided over its largest famine – and even then, life expectancy rose 20 years over the course of his rule. He launched rebellions – against a government he already controlled. He purged his enemies and friends alike.




Some 50 years after his death, he remains a central figure in Chinese politics. The Communist Party of China posthumously declared him to be 70% right and 30% wrong, but his face still hangs over Tiananmen Square.




In this second episode on China’s history, Rebecca Karl – author of 

China’s Revolutions in the Modern World –

 returns to tell Richard Hames about the Mao era, with all its promises, contradictions and catastrophes.

title: Berlin’s Plan to Take Back Homes Will Cost Europe’s Biggest Landlord £7bn
content:
Europe’s largest residential landlord is set to lose €8.4bn (£7bn) as a result of plans by leftwing political party Die Linke to bring more than 140,000 Berlin flats into public ownership.




The real estate company Vonovia, which owns roughly 130,000 apartments in the city and 

528,000

Financial Times.




Die Linke, which won Berlin’s state elections in September, has agreed to talks with the city’s Greens and Social Democrats as part of plans to transfer ownership of flats from companies that own more than 10,000 apartments, with the legislation scheduled to be brought forward in 2028.




Any apartments owned above that 10,000 threshold would have to be transferred into public ownership as part of the policy, with Die Linke proposing an average compensation of around €100,000 per apartment – around 40% below the market value.




Vonovia’s 130,000 Berlin properties have an average market value of $130,000, meaning the company would lose a projected $8.4bn if the legislation becomes law. title: Rogue AI Must Threaten 50 Lives Before Being Shut Down, Anthropic Suggests
content:
Anthropic is pushing legislation that would only allow the US government to shut down a rogue AI model when at least 50 people are at risk of imminent serious harm or death.

Under the bill

The rules laid out in the draft would prevent US states from enforcing tougher safety laws and make it harder for courts to put the brakes on dangerous AI systems.




They set a high threshold for federal intervention in the case of potential “catastrophic harm”. 




Federal officials, for example, would have to ascertain that any threat posed by AI was “imminent” and that no alternative could prevent catastrophe before intervening.

The draft bill reads: “The term ‘catastrophic risk’ means a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier developer’s development, storage, use or deployment of a frontier model will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or to more than $1bn in damage to… property arising from a single incident”.

title: Normal People Stars Back Sally Rooney in Letter to UK Government
content:
Hundreds of cultural figures including writers, actors and Nobel literature laureates have signed an open letter in support of Irish novelist Sally Rooney.




The letter, 

published today in the New Statesman

, calls on the UK government to overturn the ban on Palestine Action. Rooney’s support for the group has led to her books being withdrawn from sale in the UK for legal reasons. 




Among the signatories are the stars of the television adaptation of her book Normal People, Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones, as well as the show’s director Lenny Abrahamson.







“Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist,” the letter says. “Her books must be available to the public. Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country. 




“We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity.”




Other high-profile signatories include Nobel literature laureates Anne Carson, JM Coetzee and Annie Ernaux – plus bestselling authors Omar El Akkad, Amitav Ghosh, Jhumpa Lahiri, Michael Rosen, Arundhati Roy and Irvine Welsh.

content:

title: Why France’s Student Protesters Won’t Back Down
content:
On Sunday in Paris, crowds filled the major squares and thoroughfares of Place de La Republique, Boulevard de Magenta and beyond. Flares were lit and the flags of France, Palestine, political parties and unions adorned the crowd. In one placard, a hand drawn Homer Simpson told President Macron that disturbances in 2019 and 2023 were just the worst protests of his life “so far”, indicating that the movement does not intend to lie down easily.




Students have been on the march or blockading their schools since 17 September, but this time they were joined by trade unionists and yellow vest protesters supporting student demands, protesting against the rising cost of living and rejecting the upcoming austerity budget. Anything between 550,000 (according to the interior ministry) and 800,000 people (according to the unions) took to the streets across the country.




The convergence of different movements that have erupted under the Macron presidency could be heard in the songs and chants of the crowd. There was “on est la” (“we are here”) the defiant song of the “yellow vest” movement, chants of free Palestine, as well as adapted versions of songs against Macron’s pension reform which were recycled to apply to education.

title: UCL Urged to Lower Fees for Students Trapped in Gaza
content:
Five Palestinian students who won places at University College London (UCL) could miss out on their studies and remain stuck in Gaza because their scholarships don’t cover the cost of their fees. 




The students have been offered Global Masters Scholarships from UCL worth £15,000 but still can’t afford the remainder as they are being charged international fees, which can be over £40,000.




The UK government has agreed to help Gazan students offered places at UK universities leave the territory and get visas. But this support is limited to those with fully funded scholarships covering both fees and living costs.

author: Ash Sarkar
title: A Motion, a Meltdown, and an Andy Burnham-Shaped Opportunity
content:
They’re calling it the E motion heard around the world, as the fallout continues from the Green party’s ‘Zionism is Racism’ policy, passed at its conference earlier this month.




The motion has dominated the headlines since making it onto the agenda for autumn conference, eclipsing what the leadership had hoped would be the party’s trademark rent controls policy. It kicked off a briefing war, led by GPEW stalwart and second referendum-enthusiast Caroline Lucas. It also prompted 

pointed queries

 from the Equalities and Human Rights Commission.




And now, unwilling to let a good crisis pass him by, prime minister Andy Burnham has piled in, 

ruling out any future coalition

 with the Greens while the policy remains in place. Supporters of the motion may greet this news as a strategic win – distance from Labour cements the Greens’ status as an insurgent, anti-establishment force. But there are rumblings of discontent amongst parts of the Green party of England and Wales.




It’s no secret that Zack Polanski (while publicly supportive of the argument that Israel’s displacement of, and genocide against, the Palestinians is the result of racist ideology) needed this motion like he needed a hole in the head. He was careful to neither unequivocally back nor deride the motion, and warned that it may “create a distraction” by putting Green members and pro-Palestine activists in a position of being attacked.




Whatever the virtues of the motion were, and still might be, Polanski was proved right on this latter point. The days leading up to his unsuccessful attempt to become the MP for Holborn and St Pancras were a storm of negative media coverage, in which he was forced to defend his party against accusations of being a threat to Jewish people. It would be wrong to characterise the byelection loss as a direct result of the ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion. But it didn’t exactly help his efforts to get elected either.




What followed were the first stirrings of Green infighting. For those steeped in the factional bloodletting of Labour party politics, this is all fairly tame stuff: Lucas, the night of the count, 

failing to shut down talk

 of Polanski stepping down, Ellie Chowns 

calling on her leader to “step up”

. But while the Greens might put the ‘civil’ in civil war, this level of publicly-litigated internal division is new for the party.




What’s more, local Green parties and councils have had to manage the reactions of a significant number of Jewish residents and organisations. Haringey council, led by the Greens, found its attempts at overture 

knocked back

 by one local synagogue. “We take it from both the tone and the content of your email that you are deeply embarrassed with the decision taken by your party,” wrote Highgate United Synagogue. “[Your] embarrassment is not enough. If you really want us to feel you do not agree with the racist and genocidal implications of your party’s policy, the least we can expect is for you to publicly resile yourself from that policy and commit yourself and your party colleagues to reverse that policy.”




Enter one Andrew Burnham. Though the early months of his premiership have been marked by his attempts to mend fences with voters alienated from Labour by the party’s moral turpitude on Palestine, the temptation to kick his progressive rivals while they’re down was seemingly too much to resist.




Condemning the motion in the House of Commons at this week’s PMQs, 

Burnham thundered

: “It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it.” Polanski, in a statement, hit back, pointing out that he’s the only Jewish leader of a political party and himself a victim of antisemitism – while the prime minister “arms a genocide and locks pensioners up for opposing it”.




Westminster grandstanding has since filtered down to local governance. Yesterday, Labour issued an ultimatum, saying it would scrap any power-sharing deals with Greens in local authorities unless local Green electeds reject the ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion passed by members at conference. According to the New Statesman, such agreements prop up 

more than a dozen local authorities

, including in Bristol. Nice gauntlet you’ve got there, shame if anyone threw it.




Perhaps Alanis Morissette might have something to say about a devolution-loving prime minister imposing the will of the Westminster government on local authorities the minute he thinks it’s advantageous to do so. It’s worth pointing out that it has every chance of backfiring on the Labour party – there are few voters who want to see local government dysfunction inflicted in the name of protecting Israel’s state ideology. Labour lost votes over Gaza, and it might prove unwise for Burnham to remind people of that particular issue.




But we’re at a moment where the interests of Green electeds, and some Green activists, are at odds. The May 2026 breakthrough was powered by thousands of Green members – doorknocking, canvassing, leafleting, and getting out the vote. But that very achievement, getting Greens into councils where they might advance the eco-socialist cause by delivering for voters, is easily imperilled by that selfsame membership attempting to remodel the party in their image. That’s a tension: and one that Burnham is determined to exploit.




You can see how this puts Polanski in an invidious position. On the one hand, there’s making and protecting electoral gains, and establishing the Green party’s credibility by governing effectively. On the other, there’s standing with his members when they’re under ferocious attack by the British establishment (even if he’d rather not have picked this particular battle). But perhaps the looming interest of the EHRC, who wrote to the Greens citing the “many Jewish people [feeling] vulnerable” as a result of the motion, might hint at a way out.




Should the Greens face legal challenge, or EHRC investigation, the tactical case for reintroducing the amendments aimed at protecting Jewish members within the party gets stronger. If Polanski backs it wholeheartedly for spring conference, he might just find a way of mitigating the attack lines on antisemitism – and get back to the things he’d much rather talk about.

title: Inside Huawei: the Company That Terrifies the West
content:
Huawei makes the pipes and cables that power the Chinese internet. Its global reach has made China into a superpower.




Huawei is often accused of spying for China. But how was the US so sure that Huawei’s technology could be used for spying? Because they had already hacked it and were using it to spy themselves.




That’s not even the strangest episode in the company’s history. Its installations were bombed by the UK and US in Iraq before 9/11. In 2018, its infrastructure allegedly pinged back the secrets of the Africa Union to China overnight. And it now stands accused of doing business in Iran.




Eva Dou is the author of the deeply researched 

House of Huawei: The Secret History of China’s Most Powerful Company

.




She spoke to Richard Hames about the geopolitics of telecommunications, how Huawei made China into a global superpower, and whether or not Huawei is, in fact, a wing of the Chinese state.

“In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence,” the committee said. “Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time.”




The committee said it had been unable to contact Pillay, who serves as a judge at the UN’s international court of justice, before announcing her win on Friday morning. 




When colleagues at the Nuremberg Forum told the 85-year-old the news, Pillay joked: “Is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it.”

title: Police Spent £320k on Face ID Tech That Achieved Nothing
content:
British Transport Police (BTP) have spent more than £320k and almost 100 hours of officers’ time on a six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in London’s railway stations – yielding just one incorrect face match and no arrests. 




The surveillance tech scans passersby and alerts authorities if it recognises someone on a watchlist. It is supposed to help catch people accused of crimes or who breach court orders.




But a freedom of information request 

by Liberty Investigates

, 

shared with the Guardian

Despite this failure, Transport for London (TfL) has given permission for the technology to be expanded across London Underground stations too. 




TfL said the technology could make a vital contribution to tackling violence against the capital’s women and girls, whose travel experiences are too-often “shaped by experiences of sexual harassment and sexual offences”.

title: Trauma Farming: the New Politics of Public Suffering
content:
Are we in the era of trauma Top Trumps? ‘Lived Experience’ has become a byword for standpoint authority and progressive politics. It has allowed people from marginalised groups to speak and be heard, and forced us to confront how power plays out in interpersonal dynamics. But it has also become a way for people to brand themselves online, and excuse antisocial or even downright nasty behaviours. Has ‘lived experience’ helped the left, or turned us into self-obsessed therapy-speakers, incapable of communicating with the majority of people?




At the latest Downstream IRL, Ash Sarkar sat down with Catherine Liu – cultural theorist, professor and author of Virtue Hoarders – to discuss her new book, Traumatized: The New Politics of Public Suffering. Liu argues that as class politics has declined, the language of psychology has stepped in to explain problems rooted in capitalism. But what happens when trauma becomes content and politics gives way to what Liu calls the ‘gentrification of pain’? Is ‘lived experience’ a prerequisite for legitimate political analysis? Why do movements so often end up policing each other rather than confronting power? And if politics becomes about who’s hurting most, who benefits?

author: Novara Media
title: Secrets of the Chinese Internet
content:
Welcome to Series 2 of Do Your Own Research. Until the end of the year, I will be focusing on the most important and interesting country in the world: China.




We’re starting with Tianyu Fang, an editor of Chaoyang Trap, a newsletter all about the Chinese internet.




We’re starting with the internet because that’s so much of what we see of China: fragments of life online. What’s the reality behind them, and how do we square these beguiling, details with the vast story of China’s rise?




What is happening online in China is often reduced to a few memes or movements. We see the dazzling skyline and we stop thinking, and start gawping: that’s what I call the gawp-zone. How do we get out of it?




In this conversation, we go far deeper, into the circuits and technology of the Chinese internet, from its earliest utopian moments to the hemisphere-spanning computing stack we see today.




And we’ll be making our map of everything that has ever mattered and ever will: this new edition focused on China, available here: novaramedia.com/dyor

title: Burnham to Ban Airlines From Charging Parents to Sit With Their Children
content:

The new rule, expected to come into force before next year’s summer holidays, will apply to parents or other accompanying adults travelling with under-14s. Passengers will also have the right to correct errors on their booking free of charge.




“Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple,” Burnham said. “And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either. People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them.”

title: Greens to Announce Plan for ‘Emergency Brake’ on Rent Hikes
content:
Green party leader Zack Polanski will set out plans for a three-year emergency brake on rent hikes to give renters “breathing space”.




The move would limit rises to whichever is lowest between Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation, wage growth or 2% – echoing existing metrics for pensions, which currently increase by the highest of either inflation, wage growth or 2.5%.




Under the proposal, landlords would not be able to put up rents by more than the lowest of the three measures, which the Greens say would protect tenants from being forced out by sudden rent hikes.




Addressing delegates at the Green party conference in Brighton on Friday, Polanski will also set out plans for a “fair rents guarantee” that would keep rents “fair and affordable” once the emergency brake expires after three years.




The party says the temporary cap would give wages time to catch up with rents, which have risen faster than incomes.




“For too long, landlords have been able to hike prices way beyond wages,” Polanski is expected to say.




“That’s why today I’m calling for a three-year emergency brake on private rents. No rent rises above CPI, wage growth or 2% – whichever is lower. No sudden hikes. No evictions under the guise of rent rises. No more fear and uncertainty.”

title: Spain’s Tenants’ Rights Protesters Win Reforms After 87-Year-Old Evicted
content:
Spain’s government has approved new measures to support tenants’ rights following widespread protests – but they need approval from congress and campaigners say they do not go far enough. 




Around 30,000 people marched through Madrid on Saturday, and 

hundreds remained for days

 in encampments across the capital’s central plazas, after an 87-year-old woman was forcibly removed from her home of 70 years on a stretcher. 




Maricarmen Abascal was evicted after her rent rose from €500 (£428) to €1,650 

and she was unable to pay

. Urbagestión – the investment firm that owns the property – has now been forced to allow her to return and pay €533 in rent.  




The eviction prompted the Madrid Tenants’ Union to draw up the Maricarmen decree, which calls for a law against evicting vulnerable individuals without offering them alternative housing. It also proposes curbing unjustified price increases, a freeze on rents and an automatic renewal of leases to prevent unjustified evictions. 




Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government approved the extension of rental contracts, the ban on evicting vulnerable renters and the regulation of seasonal and room rentals that interfere with the supply of affordable housing, although measures must now be approved in congress, where the coalition lacks a majority.

title: Stop Helping Saudi Arabia Bomb Yemen, Rights Experts Tell Burnham
content:
Rights experts have urged prime minister Andy Burnham to reverse a decision to refuel Saudi Arabian warplanes as they bomb Yemen.




An open letter to Burnham and foreign secretary Ed Miliband said the UK risks being “complicit in further war crimes” after the government announced last week it would support the Saudi dictatorship’s latest attacks. 




The 

letter is signed by NGOs

It notes the Saudi-led coalition, which the UK first joined in 2015, “stands credibly accused of using starvation as a war tactic” against Yemen and of “widespread attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.” 




The UN estimates 377,000 were killed in the war on Yemen – which involved 25,000 Saudi-led air raids – between 2015 and 2022, when a ceasefire was announced. 




The new Saudi bombing campaign began after the Houthis seized large areas of land along the Red Sea coast, giving them more leverage over a crucial global shipping route.  




Recent escalation by the Houthis, the letter argues, has been driven by Israel’s UK-backed genocide in Gaza – which saw the Houthis enforce a naval blockade against Israel from 2023 – as well as the illegal US-Israeli war on Iran, a key Houthi ally.

title: Police Broke Teeth and Bones of Students at US Encampments for Gaza
content:
Thousands of pro-Palestine students were arrested on US college campuses, as part of a “widespread, McCarthyite censorship and retaliation campaign”, 

a new report has found

.




Threatened with funding cuts by the Trump administration, colleges and universities across the US played an active role in suppressing pro-Palestinian solidarity, with many students and scholars facing expulsions and deportations.




The report from the American Civil Liberties Union and Amnesty International USA, concludes that universities and law enforcement agencies acted unlawfully during the nationwide crackdown on student-led pro-Palestinian activism.




“Colleges and universities violated basic free speech, association and assembly rights and caused serious harm when they summoned campus police and local law enforcement, resulting in arrests and unlawful and unnecessary use of force,” the report says. 




The report, which spans two years of protests and their aftermath, examined 80 universities across 28 states and Washington DC, and brings together existing research combining documentary evidence with interviews and testimony to identify a broader pattern of repression.




It says universities and law enforcement repeatedly used “heavy-handed and excessive” measures against largely peaceful pro-Palestinian protesters, noting that some students had their teeth and bones broken by police

title: Prosecutors Asked to Consider Manslaughter Charges Over Grenfell Fire
content:
Police investigating the Grenfell Tower fire have submitted evidence to the Crown Prosecution Service, paving the way for potential criminal charges.




The Metropolitan Police’s investigation into the fire in North Kensington has identified 54 individuals and 20 companies and organisations. The CPS will now consider whether to move forward with prosecution.




The offences include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, fraud, health and safety offences, as well as misconduct in public office.




The Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC), the council responsible for Grenfell, is among the organisations facing criminal charges.




Almost a decade after the fire, which claimed the lives of 72 people on 14 June 2017, no charges have been brought.




The files submitted today cover all but three of the individuals the Met had said it had identified as being potentially criminally responsible back in 

May.




The CPS has said it is committed to making a decision regarding charges ahead of the 10th anniversary of the fire next year, with trials unlikely to begin before 2029.




As part of its investigation, the police looked into more than 15,000 people and 700 organisations, took 14,700 statements and gathered 165 million electronic files and more than 27,000 physical exhibits.

title: UK Universities Set to Strike in ‘Last-Ditch Fight Over Existential Cuts’
content:
University lecturers are set to walk out over “existential” cuts and course closures, as thousands of students face major disruptions as the new academic year begins.




At least eight universities have announced industrial action for the coming year, including three Russell Group institutions.




At Edinburgh, staff are striking for five weeks to protest £140m of cuts, 1,800 potential job losses and management’s refusal to rule out compulsory redundancies.




The university has also announced that 90 degree programmes will be scrapped from 2027.

title: Porn Addiction Defines Our Political Age. Here’s How.
content: The effect of pornography on the people who consume it is often moralised about, generally due to its influence over the nascent sexuality of young men. This week’s guest, investigative reporter for the Financial Times, Patricia Nilsson, has written a new book unearthing exactly the ways in which these underexamined forces emerged and how they continue to exert influence on society. She spoke to Ash about pioneering camgirl entrepreneurs, the sado-masochistic-inflected rise of Andrew Tate, and how algorithms have entered the bedroom.

content:

Green leader Zack Polanski is fighting a byelection in suboptimal conditions: in a seat with an 11,000 Labour majority, his approval ratings in a slump, and, unlike when the party won Gorton and Denton in February, a prime minister in Downing Street who not everyone totally hates. “Enough is enough. For years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti’s cancellations, delays, overcrowding and a service that has failed them time and time again,” prime minister Andy Burnham 

said in a statement

 on Sunday. 




Re-nationalising the service “means passengers, not shareholders, will come first,” he added. “More investment, fewer delays and a renewed focus on getting the basics right. We’re putting essential services back in public hands and building a railway that actually works for the people who use it.”




Avanti runs services to destinations including London, Manchester, Blackpool, Edinburgh and Birmingham.

The campaign of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has filed an appeal with the social media giant and is awaiting an explanation for the incident, state-run 

Agência Brasil reported

Lula, 80, is running for a fourth and final term against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil’s former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro. 




The controversy over the Facebook ads comes after Amnesty International accused Meta of failing to stop the spread of election-related misinformation on the platform. 




The rights group 

ran an experiment in September

 where it submitted 14 ads to Facebook that contained disinformation and “were designed to reflect… tactics that are often used by politicians and candidates to support authoritarian practices.” 




Amnesty’s test ads contained incorrect information on when and where to vote and which candidates were running, Amnesty said, as well as false allegations that “certain candidates were rigging the election”.

content:

chatting to locals

title: Ireland Goalkeeper Boycotts Match Against Israel
content:
Ireland goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu boycotted the squad’s Uefa Nations League fixture against Israel on Sunday to protest the ongoing genocide in Gaza. 




Bazunu took the decision to sit out the game in Hungary after a majority of players reportedly voted to play, despite intense pressure inside Ireland for them to respect 

calls for a sporting boycott

“My decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong,” Bazunu wrote on Instagram. “It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community, but against the atrocities in the region.

content:

title: Outsourcing Giants Made £6bn in Profit From UK’s Public Services Last Year
content:
Outsourcing companies made an estimated £6bn in profit from public services last year, with close to 11% of all public expenditure going to these private firms.




A new report

 by the think tank Common Wealth found that the public sector spent £129bn on services provided by outsourcing firms, despite the Labour government pledging to bring more public services in-house.




Since the 1980s, private companies have increasingly been brought in to run services once offered by the state. It was hoped that these supposedly efficient firms could break up cumbersome state-owned monopolies. 




But the influx of private companies has just created new monopolies. Serco – which has a £2bn contract with the Royal Navy and also manages 

public bicycle hire schemes

 – gets 90% of its global revenue from public sector contracts, according to Common Wealth’s research.
